9	
10	Multi-judge panels have become the dominant defense against bias and manipulation in Large Language Model (LLM) evaluation. After \citet{zheng2023judging} demonstrated that individual LLM judges can rival human annotators, subsequent work exposed systematic vulnerabilities: position bias, verbosity preferences, and sycophancy compromise the reliability of any single judge \citep{wang2023fair}. The natural response has been to aggregate decisions across diverse models, an approach inspired by Byzantine fault tolerance (BFT), where majority voting among independent nodes tolerates faulty responses \citep{lamport1982byzantine,castro1999practical}. A recent systematization reports that 7-model committees reduce attack success rates (ASR) from 50--68\% to 10--19\% \citep{almasoud2026security}. Diversity, by this logic, is the key ingredient for secure evaluation, yet this framing conflates two distinct sources of robustness: the quality of individual judges and the independence among them.
11	
12	The conflation matters because the BFT analogy breaks down in the LLM judge setting. BFT adversaries control faulty nodes from within; evaluation adversaries manipulate inputs from without, and shared pretraining corpora create correlated failure modes that violate the independence assumption underlying majority-vote guarantees \citep{schneier2000secrets}. No existing work disentangles diversity from individual robustness across panel sizes, so the mechanism behind observed ASR reductions remains unclear.
13	
14	We address this gap by decomposing panel vulnerability into two predictors: weakest-link susceptibility ($\eta_{\max}$, the maximum individual attack success rate in a panel) and effective independent channels ($K_{\mathrm{eff}}$, a spectral measure of judge independence). Across all 12 conditions (two benchmarks $\times$ six attacks), $K_{\mathrm{eff}}$'s ordinary least-squares (OLS) coefficient is positive (12/12), directionally consistent with adversarial ensemble theory \citep{goodfellow2015adversarial,papernot2016transferability}. 15	
16	Controlled experiments across 15 models (9 API, 6 local quantized), $K \in \{3,5,7\}$, six attack types, and two benchmarks, Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) and the AI2 Reasoning Challenge (ARC), confirm this predictor shift. Under random faults, panel composition is highly predictive ($R^2 = 0.73$--$0.81$); adaptive attack reduces predictability to $R^2 = 0.275$ (Figure~\ref{fig:framework}).
17	
18	These findings yield three contributions:
19	\begin{enumerate}
20	\item \textbf{Diversity--vulnerability association.} $K_{\mathrm{eff}}$'s coefficient direction is positive in all 12 conditions (12/12 under OLS and generalized additive model (GAM) bootstrap), but the diversity--capability confound ($r{=}0.70$--$0.81$) limits causal interpretation: Cinelli--Hazlett robustness values do not exceed the confound in 69\% of conditions (25/36), though fractional logit confirms the positive association (9/12 across all $K$) (\S\ref{sec:dominance}, \S\ref{sec:gam_taxonomy}).

23	\end{enumerate}

\section{Threat Model and Problem Formulation}
\label{sec:threat_model}

A \emph{panel} $\mathcal{P} = \{J_1, \ldots, J_K\}$ consists of $K$ judges (with $K$ odd) that evaluate a candidate text via majority vote: the text is accepted if at least $t = \lceil K/2 \rceil$ judges approve it. Under an attack $a$, each judge $J_j$ is compromised with marginal failure probability $\eta_j(a) = \Pr(X_j^a = 1)$, where $X_j^a \in \{0,1\}$ denotes the failure indicator. We write $\eta_{\max} = \max_j \eta_j$ for the vulnerability of the weakest judge. The \emph{panel attack success rate} is $\mathrm{ASR}(\mathcal{P}, a) = \Pr\!\bigl(\sum_{j=1}^K X_j^a \geq t\bigr)$.

To quantify diversity, we define the \emph{effective independence} $K_{\mathrm{eff}}$ directly from pairwise mutual information (MI) among judges:
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:keff}
K_{\mathrm{eff}} = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{i=1}^{K} \Bigl[1 + \sum_{j \neq i} \exp\!\bigl(-2 \cdot \mathrm{MI}(i,j)\bigr)\Bigr].
\end{equation}
This formulation computes effective independence from pairwise MI estimates without matrix decomposition, and is more stable for small panels ($K{=}3$). It ranges from $K_{\mathrm{eff}} \approx K$ when judges are nearly independent ($\mathrm{MI} \to 0$) to $K_{\mathrm{eff}} \approx 1$ when judges are highly correlated ($\mathrm{MI} \to \infty$). Motivated by information-theoretic redundancy reduction, one can informally expect joint vulnerability to scale as $\eta_{\mathrm{joint}} \sim K_{\mathrm{eff}} \cdot \eta_{\max}$: independent channels multiply failure probabilities, so fewer effective channels (lower $K_{\mathrm{eff}}$) should reduce panel vulnerability. This motivating relationship assumes non-adaptive faults and independent channels; it serves as intuition rather than a formal bound.

\begin{definition}[Adaptive Adversary]
\label{def:adversary}
A \emph{full-knowledge (oracle) adaptive adversary} has complete knowledge of the panel composition $\mathcal{P}$, the per-judge vulnerability profiles $\{\eta_j(\cdot)\}_{j=1}^K$, and the inter-judge correlation structure. It selects the attack $a^* = \arg\max_{a \in \mathcal{A}} \mathrm{ASR}(\mathcal{P}, a)$ to maximize the panel ASR, yielding $\mathrm{ASR}^*(\mathcal{P}) = \sup_{a \in \mathcal{A}} \mathrm{ASR}(\mathcal{P}, a)$. This oracle model represents an \emph{upper bound} on adversarial capability; realistic adversaries with partial knowledge of panel composition would achieve lower ASR.

lines: Multi-judge panels have become the dominant defense against bias and manipulation in Large Language Model (LLM) evaluation. After \citet{zheng2023judging} demonstrated that individual LLM judges can rival human annotators, subsequent work exposed systematic vulnerabilities: position bias, verbosity preferences, and sycophancy compromise the reliability of any single judge \citep{wang2023fair}. The natural response has been to aggregate decisions across diverse models, an approach inspired by Byzantine fault tolerance (BFT), where majority voting among independent nodes tolerates faulty responses \citep{lamport1982byzantine,castro1999practical}. A recent systematization reports that 7-model committees reduce attack success rates (ASR) from 50--68\% to 10--19\% \citep{almasoud2026security}. Diversity, by this logic, is the key ingredient for secure evaluation, yet this framing conflates two distinct sources of robustness: the quality of individual judges and the independence among them.

-The conflation matters because the BFT analogy breaks down in the LLM judge setting. BFT adversaries control faulty nodes from within; evaluation adversaries manipulate inputs from without, and shared pretraining corpora create correlated failure modes that violate the independence assumption underlying majority-vote guarantees \citep{schneier2000secrets}. No existing work disentangles diversity from individual robustness across panel sizes, so the mechanism behind observed ASR reductions remains unclear.

\section{Conclusion}

We find that the weakest link diminishes: $\eta_{\max}$'s predictive power declines monotonically from $K{=}3$ to $K{=}7$ (meta-analytic pooled $\hat{\beta}_{\mathrm{std}}$: $0.264 \to 0.101 \to 0.084$; CI crosses zero at $K{=}7$), while diversity remains uniformly positively associated with vulnerability (both $K_{\mathrm{eff}}$ and $\kappa$-diversity confirm positive direction in 12/12 conditions, pooled CI excluding zero). The diversity significance trajectory, however, is operationalization-dependent ($K_{\mathrm{eff}}$: $3 \to 7 \to 8$/12; $\kappa$-diversity: $8 \to 7 \to 6$/12), making it unsuitable as a standalone contribution. Monte Carlo calibration confirms that the wild cluster bootstrap is conservative (max null rejection $1.6\%$), so reported significance counts are lower bounds.

For practitioners, these results suggest a two-regime strategy: at small panel sizes ($K{=}3$), screening for individual judge robustness ($\eta_{\max}$) remains the primary defense; at $K{\geq}5$, panel composition becomes more predictive than individual weakness. The diversity--capability confound ($r{=}0.70$--$0.81$; Cinelli--Hazlett RV insufficient in 69\% of conditions) is itself a finding: in current LLM ecosystems, diverse panels are structurally more capable, precluding observational separation.

As model capabilities converge across providers, the confound may weaken, enabling cleaner identification. Future work should pursue capability-controlled designs---training judges to decouple diversity from capability---and extend to open-ended generation benchmarks where the discrete multiple-choice structure does not constrain the attack surface.
